# Exact sector areas and chord endpoints with one new vertex per sector

## 1. Statement and distinction from the archived replacement

Let K be a planar convex body with 0 in its interior. Let R_1,...,R_m be distinct rays from 0 in cyclic order, whose consecutive angular gaps are strictly less than pi. Write

    P_i=boundary(K) intersect R_i,
    S_i=cone(P_i,P_(i+1)),

with cyclic indices. Choose, independently at each P_i, one actual supporting line L_i of K.

**Theorem.** There is a planar convex polygon Q such that:

1. 0 is in int Q and boundary(Q) intersect R_i=P_i for every i.
2. |Q intersect S_i|=|K intersect S_i| for every i.
3. Each chosen line L_i still supports Q at P_i.
4. In the open sector between R_i and R_(i+1), the boundary of Q has at most ONE vertex.

Thus Q has at most 2m boundary vertices. For the six rays of three distinct lines through 0, Q has at most 12 vertices. It preserves exactly the six ray endpoints, all six sector areas, total area, all three central chords, and the areas of all six oriented halfspaces determined by those lines.

This strengthens the finite-data scope in `candidate 98181ddbde71e951`: that source preserves arrangement-cell areas by an unrestricted finite polygon, whereas the present theorem also fixes the actual chord endpoints and gives a uniform vertex bound. The present construction does not assert arbitrarily close Hausdorff approximation. It makes no claim that replacing one mixed fiber preserves its compatibility with the other fibers or its depth in unrecorded directions.

## 2. The complete shape of an actual endpoint wedge

Fix consecutive endpoints P,Q. Use the linear coordinates

    w=x P+y Q.

The sector is x,y>=0, and its endpoints are (1,0),(0,1). The determinant of this coordinate map is positive and nonzero. The chosen supporting lines have containing halfplanes

    phi_P(x,y)=x+p y<=1,
    phi_Q(x,y)=q x+y<=1.                         (1)

These normalizations exist because 0 is strictly inside K, so the original support values are positive. Since both endpoints belong to K, p<=1 and q<=1; negative p or q are allowed.

Define the possibly unbounded endpoint wedge

    W={x,y>=0:x+p y<=1, q x+y<=1}.                (2)

The actual sector piece lies in W and contains the core triangle conv{0,(1,0),(0,1)}. We classify W explicitly.

If p=1 or q=1, then W is exactly the core triangle, because one inequality is x+y<=1 and the other is automatic there.

Otherwise p,q<1. Put D=1-pq. If D>0, the two support lines meet at

    E=((1-p)/D,(1-q)/D).

Both coordinates are positive and

    E_x+E_y-1=(1-p)(1-q)/D>0.

Taking the positive linear combination with coefficients (1-q)/D and (1-p)/D of the two support inequalities bounds x+y by E_x+E_y. Thus W is bounded, and its four vertices are 0,(1,0),E,(0,1). Its area is

    |W|=(E_x+E_y)/2.                            (3)

If D<=0, both p and q must be negative: neither a positive product of two numbers in [0,1), nor a nonpositive product, can be at least one. The strictly positive vector

    v=(-p,1)

satisfies phi_P(v)=0 and phi_Q(v)=D<=0. It is therefore a recession direction of W. In particular x+y is unbounded on W. This accounts for parallel and divergent endpoint supports without a general-position assumption.

## 3. Exact sector area with just one additional point

Let alpha be the actual area of K in this sector, measured in the coordinates of Section 2. Thus the ordinary area is alpha times det(P,Q). We have alpha>=1/2 because K contains the core triangle, and alpha<=|W| when W is bounded.

We construct a point V=(u,v) in W, with u,v>0, such that

    u+v=2alpha.                                  (4)

Let M=(1/2,1/2). If alpha=1/2, take V=M. If W is bounded and not the core triangle, use (3) to set

    theta=(2alpha-1)/(E_x+E_y-1),
    V=(1-theta)M+theta E.

The parameter belongs to [0,1], so V is in W and has strictly positive coordinates. If W is unbounded, use the recession vector from Section 2 and set

    V=M+[(2alpha-1)/(1-p)](-p,1).

Again V is in W, both coordinates are positive, and (4) holds. These are finite explicit choices; no infimum, limit, or unattained area parameter is used.

Define the replacement sector piece

    Q_sector=conv{0,(1,0),V,(0,1)}.               (5)

Because u,v>0 and u+v>=1, the indicated cyclic order is convex; equality gives the core triangle with a redundant V. The piece remains in the actual endpoint wedge, preserves both axis endpoints, and its area is exactly

    |Q_sector|=(u+v)/2=alpha.                    (6)

It has at most one vertex in the open sector.

We record its explicit gauge on the sector. Set

    p'=(1-u)/v,   q'=(1-v)/u,
    f_sector(x,y)=max{x+p'y, q'x+y},  x,y>=0.     (7)

This has Q_sector as its unit sublevel. If u+v=1 then p'=q'=1. Otherwise p',q'<1 and 1-p'q'=(u+v-1)/(uv)>0, so the classification of Section 2 verifies the sublevel directly. The gauge is positive away from 0, finite, continuous, convex on its sector, and positively homogeneous.

Moreover V in W implies p<=p' and q<=q'. Consequently

    f_sector>=phi_P,  f_sector>=phi_Q             (8)

throughout the sector. It equals the radial coordinate on both bounding rays. These common lower support functions ensure convexity when the sectors are joined.

## 4. Gluing the sectors without losing convexity

Perform Section 3 in every S_i, always using the SAME selected line L_i at P_i for both adjacent sectors. Let Q_i be the resulting sector piece and define f by its sector gauges (7), with f(0)=0.

Let phi_i denote the globally defined linear functional for L_i, normalized by

    L_i={w:phi_i(w)=1},
    K subset {w:phi_i(w)<=1}.

On a shared ray R_i the two adjacent definitions satisfy

    f(t P_i)=t=phi_i(tP_i), t>=0.                (9)

They also both dominate phi_i, by (8). Thus f is globally continuous.

To prove global convexity, consider any line not passing through 0. On each sector its restriction is convex and piecewise linear. At a crossing of R_i, the two adjacent restrictions lie above the SAME affine function phi_i and agree with it at the crossing. Hence the left derivative of f is at most the derivative of phi_i, while its right derivative is at least that derivative. The slope therefore cannot decrease at the join.

There are finitely many crossings and finitely many linear pieces on the line. Its restriction is continuous and piecewise linear with nondecreasing slopes, so it is convex. On a line through 0, positive homogeneity makes each of its two half-line restrictions linear. The slopes through 0 are -f(-e) and f(e) for a directed unit vector e. Positivity away from 0 gives -f(-e)<=f(e), so this restriction is convex as well. Consequently f is convex on every line, which is precisely convexity on the plane.

It follows that

    Q={w:f(w)<=1}=union_i Q_i                  (10)

is convex. It is bounded because each of the finitely many sector pieces is bounded. It contains 0 in its interior: f is continuous and bounded on the unit circle, so a sufficiently small disk has f<1.

The convex union in (10) is a polygon, equal to the convex hull of the union of the finite vertex sets of its pieces. Equation (9) preserves every ray endpoint, and (6) preserves every sector area. There is at most one new boundary vertex in each open sector, plus the m prescribed ray points; some of those points may become redundant, which only lowers the count.

Finally each L_i is a global supporting line of Q. Near P_i, both adjacent pieces lie in its containing halfplane, and P_i belongs to Q. If a point of the convex Q lay on its other side, the segment from that point to P_i would give points arbitrarily close to P_i on the wrong side, contradicting the local containment. This proves the support-line assertion and completes the theorem.

## 5. Consequences for three central chords and finite cap data

For three distinct lines through an interior source, translate the source to 0 and list the six rays cyclically. Their consecutive angular gaps are strictly less than pi. The theorem applies directly, retaining all six endpoints and the chosen actual supporting line at each endpoint.

Each central chord is the interval between its two retained opposite endpoints. Its Euclidean length, and its normalized length after division by any fixed nonzero normal length, are unchanged. Each oriented closed halfspace determined by one of the three lines is the union of three open sectors plus boundary rays. Rays have area zero, so all its cap areas are unchanged. Total area is the sum of all six sector areas.

Thus every condition involving only these recorded areas and central sections has an exact polygonal representative with at most 12 vertices. This includes a fixed three-cap profile and its three normalized inverse-section weights. It is a finite-dimensional geometric reduction, not a reduction to triangles or a classification of an extremizer.

The new vertices can lie outside K, and original points can be removed. Therefore this ordinary replacement cannot be applied to an induced mixed-integer family while silently retaining all inter-fiber convexity conditions. Such an application requires a separate compatibility proof.

## 6. Supplementary exact geometric verification

The verifier `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_fixed_endpoint_sector_polygon_replacement_slab_recovery.py` passes **32,735 exact rational checks** on actual convex input polygons. It checks the complete reconstructed polygon, its global convexity, every original endpoint support line, all six ray endpoints, all six sector areas, all six cap areas, and total area. The inputs exercise core, bounded-wedge, and genuinely unbounded-wedge cases. These computations are independent consistency checks on the explicit construction; the arbitrary-body theorem is proved in Sections 1–4.
